client: Hey Luna. I guess I should start by saying I'm not totally convinced this will help, but I'm willing to try. Since graduating last May, I've been sending out resumes constantly but can't land a job in marketing like most of my classmates have. Seeing them post about their new jobs on LinkedIn makes me feel like a complete failure. I keep wondering what's wrong with me that no one wants to hire me.
therapist: It sounds like you're feeling really discouraged in your job search, especially when comparing yourself to your classmates. That self-doubt about "what's wrong with me" seems particularly painful. I notice you're speaking quickly and softly - would you say there's some anxiety mixed in with these feelings of frustration?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client:
Yeah, the anxiety is definitely there. Every time I see another classmate post about their new job on LinkedIn, my stomach just knots up. I try to tell myself it's not a competition, but it's hard not to feel like I'm falling behind somehow. 

The worst part is when I get a rejection email - I immediately start thinking maybe I'm just not good enough compared to everyone else. I know that's probably not true, but the thoughts keep coming anyway.
therapist: Your voice sounds particularly tense when you describe those rejection emails - it seems like those moments really hit you hard. While you logically know you're not "not good enough," I'm hearing how powerful that automatic thought feels in the moment. Would you be willing to explore what specifically makes those rejections so painful for you?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: It's just...every rejection feels like proof that I'm not cut out for this career path. Even though I know logically that lots of people get rejected, in that moment it's like all my worst fears about myself are confirmed. The worst part is when they say "we went with candidates whose experience better matches our needs" - my brain twists that into meaning I'm fundamentally lacking.
therapist: I hear how those rejection messages seem to confirm your deepest fears about yourself, even though you know intellectually that they're standard responses. Your voice sounds especially strained when you talk about interpreting them as meaning you're "fundamentally lacking" - that must be exhausting to carry. What do you think might happen if you tried responding to those automatic thoughts with the same kindness you'd show a friend in your position?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

client:
I don't know... it's hard to imagine being kind to myself about this. When I think about trying, it just feels fake, like I'd be lying to myself. My friend would deserve kindness, but I don't - that's the difference. 

And honestly, even if I tried, I don't think it would change how much those rejections hurt. They still prove I'm not good enough, no matter how I try to spin it.
therapist: Your voice sounds strained and rushed when you talk about not deserving kindness - that tells me this belief runs deep. It's interesting how easily we can extend compassion to others while denying it to ourselves. What would it feel like to acknowledge that job rejections are painful, without letting them define your worth as a person?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, very quiet, very rapid speech

client: I guess I do feel a bit rushed and defensive when talking about it—it’s just hard to separate the rejections from my self-worth. It feels like every “no” confirms that I’m not good enough, even though I know logically that’s not true. I can see how I’m kinder to others in similar situations, but when it’s me, it’s like I’m holding myself to a different, harsher standard.
therapist: I hear you noticing this important pattern - how you're able to hold space for others' struggles but struggle to extend that same understanding to yourself. That awareness is actually a really valuable first step. Would you be open to exploring what might happen if you tried applying just a fraction of that kindness you'd give a friend to your own situation?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I get what you're saying, but it feels so much harder when it's about me. When a friend is struggling, it's clear what they need—comfort, reassurance, patience. But when I look at my own situation, it’s like there’s this voice in my head saying I don’t deserve that same kindness. It feels fake or forced when I try to be nice to myself. I don’t know how to shut that voice off.
therapist: It sounds like there's a real disconnect between the compassion you can so easily offer others and what you feel you deserve yourself. Your voice softens when you talk about what your friend might need, but becomes more strained when turning that same care inward. What do you think might be behind that belief that kindness toward yourself feels "fake or forced"?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, very quiet, fast speech

client: I guess I just feel like I haven’t earned kindness toward myself. When I try to be compassionate with myself, it feels like I’m pretending or letting myself off the hook for things I should be holding myself accountable for. It’s easier to be kind to others because they haven’t made the same mistakes I have.
therapist: I hear how strongly you believe kindness must be "earned," and how that makes self-compassion feel like letting yourself off the hook. Your voice rises when you talk about mistakes - it seems that idea carries a lot of weight for you. What would it look like to hold yourself accountable while also recognizing that struggling doesn't make you undeserving of kindness?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I guess I’ve always felt like kindness is something you deserve only if you’ve done something right. If I’m struggling or messing up, it feels like I should be harder on myself, not gentler. The idea of being kind to myself when I’m not doing well just feels... wrong, like I’m letting myself get away with something. I don’t know how to separate accountability from punishment. It’s confusing.
therapist: You're describing such an important distinction - between accountability that helps us grow and punishment that just makes us feel worse. I notice your voice speeds up when you talk about feeling like you're "getting away with something" - that tension between what you believe about kindness and how it applies to you seems really charged. What do you think might happen if you experimented with treating yourself with the same supportive accountability you'd offer a friend who was struggling?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: I don't know, the idea of being kind to myself makes me uncomfortable somehow. Like if I go easy on myself, I'll just become lazy or irresponsible. When I imagine talking to a friend the way I talk to myself, it does seem harsh, but I can't shake the feeling that I deserve the criticism.
therapist: It sounds like you're wrestling with this fear that self-kindness might lead to complacency, even while recognizing how harsh your self-talk has become. Your voice gets quieter when you talk about deserving criticism - that makes me wonder how long you've been carrying this belief that being hard on yourself is necessary. What do you think keeps this pattern feeling so necessary, even when you can see it might not be helping?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I guess I've always believed that if I go easy on myself, I'll stop pushing to improve. My dad was really hard on me growing up, and part of me still thinks that's what made me achieve anything at all. But it's exhausting to constantly feel like I'm not good enough, even when I know logically that's not true.
therapist: It sounds like you're carrying this belief that being hard on yourself is what drives your success, even though it comes at such an emotional cost. I hear how exhausting it must be to maintain that standard, especially when it's tied to messages from your childhood. What would it feel like to experiment with the idea that you might actually perform better if you weren't constantly weighed down by that feeling of not being good enough?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech
